report:
**Conclusion:**  
Contrary to earlier assumptions, high-quality evidence indicates that taking probiotics **does not** reliably shorten the duration of acute infectious diarrhea.

**Summary of Evidence:**
* **Older vs. Recent Findings:** While earlier meta-analyses suggested probiotics might reduce diarrhea duration by about 24 hours, these conclusions relied on smaller studies with variable methodology. Recent large, low-bias trials—such as 2018 studies published in *The New England Journal of Medicine*—found no significant benefit of probiotics over placebo for acute gastroenteritis (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802597).
* **Updated Cochrane Review:** The updated Cochrane Systematic Review incorporated these large, rigorous trials and concluded that probiotics probably make little to no difference in the number of people with diarrhea lasting 48 hours or longer, with high uncertainty regarding any reduction in overall duration (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33295643/).
* **Clinical Guidelines:** Reflecting this updated evidence, major medical bodies such as the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) updated their practice guidelines to advise against routine probiotic use for managing acute infectious gastroenteritis (https://www.gastrojournal.org/article/S0016-5085(20)34729-6/fulltext).

**Sources:**

2. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33295643/
3. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802597
4. https://www.gastrojournal.org/article/S0016-5085(20)34729-6/fulltext
